entries.title: A device is signed in to your Google account
entries.what_it_means: Whoever has this device can open your Gmail, see where you have been, and change your settings.
entries.notice_why: The device is signed out of your account. Whoever uses it will notice the next time they open Gmail or another Google app.
evidence_first: Screenshot the device list, including this device's name, place and time.
steps: Open this setting.
Select the device.
Select Sign out.
Then change your password, or they can sign back in.
entries.if_not_safe_yet: Leave it for now and screenshot it. Do not use this account for private messages until it is signed out. Talk to an advocate about when to do it.

entries.title: A phone can reset your password
entries.what_it_means: Whoever has this number can use it to get into your account, even after you change your password.
entries.notice_why: Spare Key does not know whether Google tells the old number. Whoever has it would notice if they tried to use it.
evidence_first: Screenshot the recovery phone page. The last four digits are enough to show which number it is.
steps: Open this setting.
If the number is not yours, change it to a number only you can reach, or remove it.
Google may still send codes to the old number for 7 days. Change your password and sign out other devices at the same time.
entries.if_not_safe_yet: Leave it for now and screenshot it. Tell an advocate, because this number could undo a password change.

entries.title: An app can watch and control this phone
entries.what_it_means: This app has several kinds of control over the phone, or came from outside the Play Store with one. Monitoring apps are set up this way. It may see your messages, your screen and where you are.
entries.notice_why: If the app stops reporting, whoever installed it may notice. Removing it also deletes it as evidence.
evidence_first: With another phone, take a picture of the app’s page in Settings, then Apps, including what it can do and where it was installed from.
Write down when you first noticed it, and anything that made you think someone knew things they should not.
steps: Do not delete the app yet. Take a picture of it with another phone, or write it down first.
Talk to an advocate about when to remove it.
When you are ready, open Settings, then Security and privacy, then Device admin apps, and turn the app off if it is there.
Then open Settings, then Accessibility, and turn the app off.
Then open Settings, then Apps, choose the app, and select Uninstall.
entries.if_not_safe_yet: Leave it for now. Your record from step 1 is enough. Use a phone or computer the other person has never had for anything private, including this plan. Some people keep this phone as it is and use a second phone for private things. Police can sometimes examine the phone before anything is removed, which keeps it as evidence. Talk to an advocate about which fits you, and when.

entries.title: An app can see which apps you use
entries.what_it_means: This app can see which apps you open and for how long.
entries.notice_why: Reports about which apps you use stop.
evidence_first: With another phone, take a picture of the app’s page in Settings, then Apps, including what it can do and where it was installed from.
Write down when you first noticed it, and anything that made you think someone knew things they should not.
steps: Take a picture of it with another phone, or write it down first.
Open Settings, then Apps, then Special app access, then Usage access.
Choose the app and turn it off.
entries.if_not_safe_yet: Leave it for now. Take a picture of it with another phone, or write it down. Use a phone or computer the other person has never had for anything private, including this plan. Talk to an advocate about when to change it.

entries.title: An app can see your location all the time
entries.what_it_means: This app can see where you are even when you are not using it.
entries.notice_why: Your place stops updating in this app. Someone who watches it may see your location stop or go stale.
evidence_first: With another phone, take a picture of the app’s page in Settings, then Apps, including what it can do and where it was installed from.
Write down when you first noticed it, and anything that made you think someone knew things they should not.
steps: Take a picture of it with another phone, or write it down first.
Open Settings, then Location, then App location permissions.
Choose the app and select Allow only while using the app, or Don't allow.
entries.if_not_safe_yet: Leave it for now. Take a picture of it with another phone, or write it down. Use a phone or computer the other person has never had for anything private, including this plan. Talk to an advocate about when to change it.

entries.title: USB debugging is on
entries.what_it_means: A computer connected to this phone by cable can install and control apps on it.
entries.notice_why: This is a phone setting, not an app. It is not known whether anyone sees when it is turned off.
evidence_first: With another phone, take a picture of the Developer options page with USB debugging showing.
steps: Open Settings, then System, then Developer options.
Turn off USB debugging, and Wireless debugging if it is on.
entries.if_not_safe_yet: Leave it for now. Take a picture of it with another phone, or write it down. Use a phone or computer the other person has never had for anything private, including this plan. Talk to an advocate about when to change it.

entries.title: This phone may be rooted
entries.what_it_means: Rooting removes the limits Android puts on apps. On a rooted phone, an app can hide from this check and from the phone's own settings, so the list may not show everything.
entries.notice_why: Undoing root means resetting the phone or putting its software back. If an app on it was sending information to someone, it stops, and they may notice that.
evidence_first: With another phone, take a picture of this result, and of Settings, then About phone.
steps: Talk to an advocate before changing anything on this phone.
Save only what you need, like photos, to an account the other person has never had.
Reset the phone to factory settings: open Settings, then System, then Reset options. A reset may not undo every kind of rooting; the maker or a phone shop can put back the original software.
Or keep this phone as it is, and use a new phone the other person has never had for anything private.
entries.if_not_safe_yet: Leave it for now, and treat this phone as one the other person can see. Use a phone or computer they have never had for anything private, including this plan. Police can sometimes examine the phone first, which keeps it as evidence. Talk to an advocate about which fits you, and when.

entries.title: Someone can see your location in Find My
entries.what_it_means: This person can see where your iPhone is, on their own phone.
entries.notice_why: Your location disappears from their Find My app, and Apple says they may notice.
evidence_first: Take a picture of the Find My People list with another phone, or write down each name.
steps: Open the Find My app and tap People.
Tap the person.
Tap Stop Sharing My Location.
entries.if_not_safe_yet: Leave it for now. Talk to an advocate before you go anywhere you want to keep private, because they can see where your phone is. Leaving the phone somewhere is one option to plan with an advocate.

entries.what_they_see: You disappear from their Find My, Maps, Contacts and Messages apps. On older iPhones they may get a message that you stopped sharing.

entries.title: Someone else runs your Apple family group
entries.what_it_means: The organizer can see what the family buys, and family members may share location and screen time.
entries.notice_why: You disappear from their family list, and shared purchases and subscriptions stop for you.
evidence_first: Take a picture of the Family list in Settings with another phone, or write down each name.
steps: Open Settings, then Family (below your name).
Tap your name.
Tap Leave Family.
entries.if_not_safe_yet: Leave it for now. In Settings, then Family, you can see who sees your location. Turning it off for one person may be noticed too. Talk to an advocate first, and about any children in the group.

entries.title: A device you do not know is signed in to your Apple Account
entries.what_it_means: Whoever has this device may see your messages, photos and where you are.
entries.notice_why: The device is signed out of your Apple Account, so whoever uses it may notice the next time they open it.
evidence_first: Take a picture of the device list with another phone, or write down each device name and model.
steps: Open Settings, then Privacy and Security, then Safety Check.
Choose Manage Sharing and Access, then review the devices.
Remove the device you do not know, then change your Apple Account password.
entries.if_not_safe_yet: Leave it for now. Keep private things out of iMessage and iCloud until it is removed. Talk to an advocate about when to do it.

entries.what_they_see: The device is signed out of your account and stops getting your messages and photos.

entries.title: Your phone warned you about a tracker moving with you
entries.what_it_means: A tracker, like an AirTag, may be in your bag, your car or something you carry, and may show someone where you are.
entries.notice_why: If the tracker is moved, turned off or stops moving with you, its owner may see that.
evidence_first: Take a picture of the alert and the map with another phone, or write down the date, the time and where you were.
steps: Open the alert and follow it to find the tracker, if you choose to.
Ask an advocate or the police what to do with it, because it is also evidence.
entries.if_not_safe_yet: Leave it for now, and talk to an advocate. Some people leave the tracker where it is until they have a plan, because moving it may be noticed.

entries.title: Someone can see your location in Life360
entries.what_it_means: People in your Life360 circle can see where you are, and where you have been.
entries.notice_why: Your place on their map stops updating, or you leave their circle, which they can see.
evidence_first: Take a picture of the circle's member list with another phone, or write down each name.
steps: Open Life360 and choose the circle.
Check who is in it.
Leave the circle, or turn off location sharing for it, when it is a good time.
entries.if_not_safe_yet: Leave it for now. Talk to an advocate before you go anywhere you want to keep private, because the circle can see where your phone is.

entries.title: Someone else holds your phone plan
entries.what_it_means: The account holder can see who you call and text, and may be able to locate the phone or move the number.
entries.notice_why: Moving your number to your own plan shows on their account and their bill.
evidence_first: Write down the carrier, the account holder and the lines on the plan, on paper or with another phone.
steps: Ask your carrier how to move your number to a plan in your own name.
Until then, use another phone for private calls and texts.
entries.if_not_safe_yet: Leave it for now. Your calls and texts may show on their account, so use another phone for private calls, like the hotline. Talk to an advocate about a free phone and when to move.
